title: Conservation of Momentum
hook: Fire a gun and it kicks back; push off a friend on skates and you both glide apart. Total momentum never changes unless an outside force interferes.
key_points: With no outside force, a system's total momentum stays constant over time.
Momentum lost by one object is exactly gained by another.
It explains recoil: a gun kicks back as the bullet shoots forward.
It powers rockets: throwing exhaust one way pushes the rocket the other way.
content_html: One of physics' most reliable rules: if no outside force acts on a system, its total momentum stays exactly the same. Objects inside can shove each other around all they like, but whatever momentum one gains, another loses by an equal amount. The grand total is locked in.
extra_html: This single principle explains a surprising range of everyday and high-tech events. A rifle and its bullet start with zero momentum; when fired, the bullet flies forward and the gun recoils backward so the two cancel out. Two skaters who push apart drift off in opposite directions for the same reason. And it's how rockets work even in the vacuum of space — there's nothing to push against, so the engine hurls exhaust gas backward and the rocket gains an equal and opposite momentum forward. Conservation of momentum holds because internal forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs, as Newton's third law guarantees. Wikipedia's section on conservation lays out the reasoning and these classic examples.

related.title: Momentum: The Quantity of Motion
related.hook: A slow freight train and a fast bullet are both brutally hard to stop. Momentum captures why: it's mass times velocity, the real measure of moving 'oomph'.

related.title: Elastic vs. Inelastic Collisions
related.hook: Billiard balls click and bounce; cars crumple and stick. Both conserve momentum, but only one keeps its energy of motion — the difference is where the energy goes.

flashcards.prompt: When is the total momentum of a system conserved?
flashcards.back_html: Whenever no net external force acts on the system. The total momentum stays the same even as objects within it push on each other.

flashcards.prompt: Two ice skaters at rest push off each other. What happens?

choices.text: They glide apart in opposite directions so total momentum stays zero
They both move the same direction
They stay put because momentum can't appear from nothing

flashcards.explanation_html: Starting at zero momentum, they must end at zero total. Equal and opposite momenta cancel, so they slide apart.

flashcards.prompt: How does a rocket accelerate in empty space with nothing to push against?

choices.text: It throws exhaust backward, so it gains equal momentum forward
It pushes against the air around it
It creates momentum from its fuel's chemical energy

flashcards.explanation_html: Conservation of momentum: the backward momentum of the exhaust is matched by the rocket's forward momentum. No outside air needed.
